title: SRP: Single Responsibility Principle
description: One reason to change: how to spot a class that does too much and how to split it without over-splitting.

questions.text: What does the Single Responsibility Principle actually say?

options.text: A function must never be longer than ten lines
A class must have exactly one method
A class should have one reason to change, because it answers to one actor or concern
Every file must contain exactly one class

questions.explanation: The principle is about reasons to change, not about counting methods or lines. A class with ten methods can follow it if they all serve the same concern; a class with two can break it if one serves finance and the other serves operations.

questions.text: An `Invoice` class calculates totals, writes itself to the database and renders a PDF. The finance team changes the tax rules and the design team changes the PDF layout. Why is this a problem?

options.text: PDF code is always slow
Two unrelated groups will edit the same class, so a change for one can break the other
Classes are not allowed to touch a database
It uses too much memory

questions.explanation: Each group is a separate reason to change. When both edit one class their changes collide in merges, share fields by accident, and a bug in the PDF code can fail a tax test. Splitting by actor keeps each change local.

questions.text: Which refactoring best fixes a `UserService` that registers users, hashes passwords, sends welcome emails and writes audit logs?

options.text: Make all the methods private
Rename it to `UserManager`
Move every method to static helpers in one `Utils` class
Keep registration in `UserService` and move hashing, email and audit into their own collaborators that it calls

questions.explanation: Registration is the one job that stays. Hashing, mailing and auditing change for different reasons, so each gets its own small class, injected into the service. A renamed class or a `Utils` dump moves the mess without separating the reasons.

questions.text: Which of these is the clearest sign that a class breaks SRP?

options.text: It implements an interface
Its constructor takes many unrelated dependencies, and tests need many mocks for one behaviour
It has a long name
It has a private field

questions.explanation: A constructor that needs a database, a mailer, a PDF engine and a clock usually means the class does several jobs. The test setup pain is the same signal seen from the other side.

questions.text: A team splits a 30-line `Order` class into twelve one-method classes "for SRP". What went wrong?

options.text: They should have used inheritance
They split by method count instead of by reason to change, so one change now touches many files
SRP forbids classes with fewer than two methods
Nothing, more classes is always better

questions.explanation: Splitting past the real seams creates shotgun surgery: a single business change must edit many tiny classes. Split along actors and concerns, and stop when each class has one reason to change.

questions.text: Two methods that always change together, for the same reason, belong in the same class even if they look like different tasks.

options.text: True
False

questions.explanation: True. Cohesion is judged by why code changes. Methods that change together for the same reason have one responsibility; separating them only adds indirection.

questions.text: Which of these are good ways to find the responsibilities in a class?

options.text: Check whether tests for one behaviour need unrelated fakes
Count the lines and split at 200
List who would ask for a change (finance, ops, design) and see how many groups appear
Describe the class in one sentence and see if it needs the word "and"

questions.explanation: Actors, the "and" test and test-setup pain all point at the real concerns. A line count is a rough smell at best; a 300-line class can be one cohesive job.

questions.text: In an HTTP endpoint, which split follows SRP best?

options.text: The controller handles HTTP, a service holds the business rule, a repository handles persistence
Everything lives in a static helper
The database does the business rules through triggers only
The controller parses the request, runs the business rules, queries SQL and formats JSON in one method

questions.explanation: HTTP translation, business rules and storage change for different reasons (API shape, policy, schema). Keeping them apart lets you swap the transport or the database without rewriting the rules.
